newsitem.title: INDIA: Cricket - Parore wants to be a lawyer after cricket.
newsitem.headline: Cricket - Parore wants to be a lawyer after cricket.

text.p: BANGALORE, May 13 - New Zealand wicketkeeper-batsman Adam Parore may be just 26 but he is already planning for a life after cricket.

Parore has committed himself to a four-year Bachelor of Law degree at Auckland University and is spending much of his down time during the Independence Cup quadrangular series in India with his head buried in law books.

"I am in my second year of the course so hopefully in another 2 1/2 years I will be ready to be unleashed on society," Parore told NZPA after a training session at Chinnaswamy Stadium here today as the Kiwis prepare for their second match in the tournament -- against hosts India on Wednesday night.
"It's one of the most interesting things I have ever done," Parore said of his legal studies.
"I find it is quite nice to have something outside of cricket to focus on.

"I can do a fair bit of studying while I am away with the cricket team. It's just a matter of organising things. I handed in some assignments and exams early before I left and I have understanding lecturers who gave me some notes in advance so I can continue studying while I am away."
A highly intelligent, complex person, Parore may well be suited to the legal profession and court room advocacy.
"I look back at all the things I have been through with the New Zealand cricket team and whether it was on the field or off the field, I have never really shied away.
"At least everyone knew where I was coming from. I've never ducked away into the background."
An often controversial figure, Parore has polarised public opinion since he made his debut for New Zealand on the tour to England in 1990.
He can at times be withdrawn, has a stubborn streak made of steel, and is very single minded. That has at times sat uncomfortably in team situations which often demand flexibility from individuals.
For Parore, the Independence Cup offers the chance in a tour situation to hone the wicketkeeping skills that saw him touted as a future international at a very early age.
Just three months ago Parore found himself on the unwanted list when he was dropped from the test team against England after a series of poor returns in the specialist No 3 batting position.
He had been converted into a specialist top order batsman by previous national coach Glenn Turner, who promoted Canterbury wicketkeeper Lee Germon to the captaincy of the New Zealand team.
It was a role Parore struggled hard to come to terms with although he achieved measured success before a slump in form saw him discarded.

But within 48 hours after being dropped as a batsman Parore was recalled for the third test against England when Germon pulled out through injury. Germon subsequently regained his fitness and place in the side for the limited overs matches against England before being axed altogether for the series against Sri Lanka in March.
The selectors instead turned, again, to Parore and no one is happier to have the job back than him.

He said he felt like a "little lost soul" during Germon's period in charge. A wicketkeeping-batsman since the age of nine, it felt like he had lost a layer of skin when he was not required to don the gloves in the field.
"I was quite ecstatic to be given the keeping role and to slot back down to seven in the batting order because that is my game and I am comfortable doing that.
"I really did miss keeping, but it is like riding a bike because you never forget how to do it.
"You just can't make wicketkeepers. If you can do it you will never forget, and if you can't do it, you will never learn."
Parore has spent a lot of time with Kiwi coach -- and former Australian gloveman -- Steve Rixon, honing his skills when standing up to the stumps to the medium paced and slow bowlers.
"It's important for the team that I am sharp when standing up, and it's very satisfying if you are doing a good job there because it is certainly the hardest aspect of wicketkeeping.
"Standing back to the faster bowlers by comparison is pretty easy really. Any reasonable athlete can do a reasonable job standing back.
Parore prides himself on his ability as both a wicketkeeper and as a batsman.
"More than anything else that I want out of this game is respect."
"When you come into this game as a young player, you have no respect from anybody. You have to earn it."
"After you have been around three or four years, opposition players start remembering and calling you by your name, and you start building a rapport with others around the circuit.
"You can tell by just looking at them whether they think you can play or not. If they bother to give you the time of day, you know they think you can play, and that is a nice feeling," Parore said.
Parore's brushes with controversy have made him wary of the media.

He said he has been "burnt a few times". He was fined and censured by New Zealand Cricket for allegedly saying the wrong things when injury forced him out of the tour of the West Indies 12 months ago.

His good looks and a previous romance with actress Greer Robson attracted the attentions of the women's magazines, and Parore's personal attitude was referred to by the Auckland selectors in February when they dropped him from their side for the latter stages of last season.
Parore's status with the Auckland association remains unclear, and as yet he does not know whether he will be playing for that province next summer.
He has maintained a low profile since Rixon assumed control of the national side at the beginning of this season, but acknowledges his public image is not what it could be.
"I accept I have a problem with my public image. I started out as a golden boy, and I'm not really sure where it went wrong.
"I understand the media now a lot more than I used to.
"I know exactly what they do for a job and I understand my job. There are times the two can't possibly meet to the best of everyone's interests."
